17985-tom-swift-and-the-visitor-from-pla:
Victor Appleton II wrote Tom Swift and the Visitor from Planet X, the seventeenth Tom Swift Jr. adventure, printed by Grosset and Dunlap. Tom Swift Jr. and his crew at Swift Enterprises wait for what may be the most important scientific event in history.

Chapters run from an earthquake and a strange hitchhiker to a Brungarian coup, a wall of water, a cave monster, and energy from Planet X. Air-borne hijackers and a kidnapping raise the stakes. Appleton writes brisk, clean science fiction for boys, full of gadgets and pluck. It is a fun, old-style Swift tale, best for young inventors.
18464-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this first volume of The Wit and Humor of America, a ten-volume library edition published by Funk and Wagnalls in New York and London, with copyrights in 1907 and 1911. The volume gathers American comic writing in prose and verse, arranged alphabetically by title.

Early pages give Holmes on the wonderful one-hoss shay, Finn on the curse of the competent, and Nye on the grammatical boy. Later entries bring Hawthorne, Riley, Stanton, Sousa, and many more, so that the book serves as a broad shelf of American humor, from dialect sketches to short poems and comic tales.
18465-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited volume two of The Wit and Humor of America, a ten-volume library edition from Funk and Wagnalls, with copyrights in 1907 and 1911. A portrait of James Whitcomb Riley fronts the volume. Wilder gathers American humor in prose and verse, from famous names and forgotten ones, for readers who want laughter with a national flavor.

Contents list Burdette's Archaeological Congress, Stowe's Aunt Dinah's Kitchen, Leland's Ballad, Hovey's Barney McGee, Tabb's Beecher Beached, and Stanton's Boy's View of It. Later pieces give a cake walk, Grandma Keeler getting Grandpa ready for Sunday school, a Hoosier and a salt pile, and a letter by Petroleum V. Nasby. Readers get American humor in bulk: dialect, satire, and domestic comedy, sampled across a generation.
18734-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this third volume of The Wit and Humor of America, published by Funk and Wagnalls, with a 1907 Bobbs-Merrill copyright and a 1911 Thwing copyright. It gathers American funny writing, from James Whitcomb Riley's Little Orphant Annie and Tree-Toad to James Russell Lowell's Courtin' and Artemus Ward's Tower of London. A frontispiece shows Samuel L. Clemens, Mark Twain.

Other pieces include Carolyn Wells on two business men, two ladies, and wild animals she has met, plus Bill Arp's Southern sketches and Gelett Burgess on Boston bohemians. The mix runs from dialect verse to comic tales and maxims. The volume is a broad, period sample of American humor.
18776-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this fourth volume of The Wit and Humor of America, published by Funk and Wagnalls, with a 1907 Bobbs-Merrill copyright and a 1911 Thwing copyright. A frontispiece shows Joel Chandler Harris, whose My Honey, My Love appears inside. James Whitcomb Riley adds Ponchus Pilut and The Raggedy Man, while Oliver Wendell Holmes offers The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table.

Other pieces include John G. Saxe's Briefless Barrister, a ballad of a lawyer with no case, Eugene Field's Story of the Two Friars, and Carolyn Wells on two husbands, two prisoners, and how to know wild animals. The mix runs from verse to dialect tale. The volume is a broad sample of American humor.
19323-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this fifth volume of The Wit and Humor of America. Funk and Wagnalls published it, with copyrights of 1907 and 1911. Contents include John Paul, James Whitcomb Riley, and Frank L. Stanton. Sol Smith, Elliott Flower, and Daniel O'Connell appear too, among many others. A note warns that this volume was not made from the library edition. So its page numbers run discontinuous.

One piece follows Mr. Gummage, a painting teacher. He paints skies red below and smoky blue above. He reverses colours on water, paints mountains lilac and white, and dabs trees with a bristle brush. Readers get a broad American humour anthology, funny, dated, and full of period flavour.
19324-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this sixth volume of The Wit and Humor of America, in ten volumes, with a portrait of Finley Peter Dunne as Mr. Dooley. It gathers American jokes, stories, and verse from Field, Riley, Thayer, Hay, and many others. Casey at the Bat and a bear story by Riley stand among the contents.

A comic piece on Sevres ware and Madame Pompadour, natural daughter of a butcher, shows the volume's chatty, digressive humour. Tales range from ballads to book canvassers and brag captains. Readers get a rich anthology of American laughter from the turn of the century.
19325-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this seventh volume of a ten-volume set of American humor, issued in the early nineteen hundreds. It gathers short pieces by many well-known writers of the day, from George Ade and Bill Nye to Eugene Field and Charles Godfrey Leland. Poems, sketches, and comic tales sit side by side.

The range is wide: small-town scenes, tall tales, dialect jokes, and sharp takes on daily life. Read in order or dipped into at random, the volume shows what made American readers laugh a century ago, and which jokes still land today.
24432-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this eighth volume of The Wit and Humor of America, in the ten-volume library edition, published by Funk and Wagnalls Company in New York and London. Its copyrights date to 1907 and 1911, and its frontispiece shows Robert J. Burdette. The volume runs from page 1399 to page 1634, gathering American wit and humor in prose and verse.

Its contents include Walt Whitman's Boston Ballad, James Montgomery Flagg's Branch Library, and James Russell Lowell's Chief Mate. Alice MacGowan's Columbia and the Cowboy, Edmund Vance Cooke's Daniel Come to Judgment, and J. T. Trowbridge's Darius Green and His Flying Machine follow, with Phoebe Cary's Day is Done, Proctor Knott's Duluth Speech, and Harold MacGrath's Enchanted Hat. Readers get American humor, volume by volume.
24433-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this ninth volume of a ten-volume anthology of American humour, published by Funk and Wagnalls. It collects poems, stories, and sketches by writers such as Bill Nye, James Whitcomb Riley, Carolyn Wells, John Habberton, and Wallace Irwin, arranged as a library of the nation's comic writing.

Pieces range from a ballad about ping-pong and a poker party to a country school sketch and a curate's encounter with a ballet girl, mixing dialect humour, parody, and light verse. The volume gives a broad, entertaining sample of what made American readers laugh around the turn of the century, and it works well dipped into a piece at a time.
24434-the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volum:
Marshall P. Wilder edited this tenth volume of The Wit and Humor of America, in the ten-volume library edition, published by Funk and Wagnalls Company in New York and London. Its copyrights date to 1907 and 1911, and its frontispiece shows Frank L. Stanton. The volume runs from page 1801 to page 2042, closing the library edition's ten volumes of American wit and humor.

Its contents include Charles Battell Loomis's Araminta and the Automobile, James Whitcomb Riley's At Aunty's House, and Frank L. Stanton's Backsliding Brother. Howard D. Sutherland's Biggs' Bar, Clinton Scollard's Bookworm's Plaint, and Charles Godfrey Leland's Breitmann in Politics follow. James Jeffrey Roche's Concord Love Song, Oliver Wendell Holmes's Contentment, and John Greenleaf Whittier's Demon of the Study close the list. Readers get the final volume of American humor.
27093-the-boy-ranchers-or-solving-the-my:
Willard F. Baker's The Boy Ranchers, or Solving the Mystery at Diamond X, published in 1921, sends Bud and his cousins Nort and Dick after a mystery on the ranch. A call for help, a mysterious search, and suspicions lead them to hit the trail after rustlers.

The boys pick over the debris of a camp, where ponies sniff for morsels, and wonder what searchers hunted without finding: no hole, no excavation, no treasure chest or hidden gold. With a professor and Del Pinzo in the mix, the book delivers a clean boys' ranch mystery in the Diamond X series.
27094-the-boy-ranchers-in-camp-or-the-wa:
Willard F. Baker's The Boy Ranchers in Camp, or The Water Fight at Diamond X, published in 1921, opens with a mysterious disappearance and a night ride. Nort's warning cry gives the frontispiece: look out, jump for your lives, it's a flood.

The boys face trouble at Square M, a strangely still reservoir, and a stopped pipe line. Nort, the eastern lad, proposes walking the old underground water-course, big enough all the way through, to find the stoppage. The book mixes camp life, flood danger, and boy detective work. The book was printed in the United States by Cupples and Leon Company. Trouble at Square M and doubling up fill the middle chapters.
4289-the-duchess-of-berry-and-the-court-:
Imbert de Saint-Amand wrote this history of the French court at the accession of Charles X. It opens on the morning of 16 September 1824. Louis XVIII lies dying at the Tuileries, and courtiers gather in the Gallery of Diana. The chapters follow the entry into Paris, the funeral, and the coronation at Rheims.

They follow the court's return to Paris. At the center stands Marie-Caroline, Duchess of Berry, with her household. Her journeys in the west and south, her theatre, and her ball recalling Mary Stuart all appear. The growing disquiet of the later 1820s closes the story, as fetes and ministries lead a glittering court toward its fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict: Benedict X was an antipope during the days of Nicholas II, whose pontificate ran from 1056 to 1061. He stood as a rival claimant to the chair of Peter against the lawful pope, in a disputed succession of the mid-eleventh century. His name survives among the antipopes of those years, marking a contested moment when rival factions pressed competing claims to the papacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement X, born Emilio Altieri at Rome on 13 July 1590, was elected on 29 April 1670 and died at Rome on 22 July 1676. After a conclave of four months and twenty days failed to elect a prominent candidate, the cardinals fell back on an aged cardinal, Altieri. He was an octogenarian whom Clement IX had raised to the purple on his deathbed. Altieri had waived earlier claims in favour of an older brother.

He protested that the papal robes were being used as a funeral shroud but accepted. He took Clement's name from gratitude to his benefactor. To save the Altieri name from extinction he adopted the Paoluzzi, marrying one to Laura Caterina Altieri, the family's sole heiress. With age he left administration to Cardinal Paoluzzi-Altieri, keeping, as Romans quipped, only blessing and sanctifying, while his Bullarium still shows canonisations of Cajetan, Francis Borgia, and Rose of Lima.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory X, born Teobaldo Visconti in 1210, was chosen after a vacancy of almost three years and reigned from 1272 to 1276. Clement IV's death in November 1268 left French and Italian cardinals deadlocked at Viterbo, neither able to win two-thirds. In summer 1270 the town's leaders locked the cardinals in the episcopal palace and cut their food, forcing a compromise.

Fifteen cardinals named six delegates, who on 1 September 1271 chose Visconti, Archdeacon of Liège, neither cardinal nor priest, then at Acre with Prince Edward on pilgrimage. Summoned home, he reached Viterbo in February 1272, accepted, and took the name Gregory X. Ordained priest on 19 March and consecrated on 27 March, he plunged into peace among Christian princes, German affairs, and clerical reform. He pursued Greek reunion and Jerusalem's deliverance, summoning the Council of Lyons for May 1274 within four days of his coronation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent X, Giambattista Pamfili, born at Rome 6 May 1574, died there 7 January 1655. His Pamfili had come from Gubbio in Umbria to Rome under Innocent VIII. He read law at the Collegio Romano and took his bachelor's degree at twenty. Clement VIII named him consistorial advocate and Rota auditor. Gregory XV posted him as nuncio to Naples, and Urban VIII dispatched him as datary to France and Spain.

Urban later named him titular Latin Patriarch of Antioch, nuncio at Madrid, and Cardinal-Priest of Sant'Eusebio in 1626, though the purple reached him only in 1629. A stormy conclave gathered 9 August 1644 to follow Urban VIII. France's faction would back no friend of Spain, and Spain's man Firenzola fell as Mazarin's foe. Dreading a French foe's rise, both sides settled on Pamfili, chosen 15 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-x:
Pope John X, Tossignano-born in Romagna, took the throne in 914 and died at Rome in 928. A deacon first, he rose to Ravenna's archbishopric about 905 after Kailo. A paper dated 5 February 914 still styles him archbishop. Soon after, Rome's ruling nobles pushed him into the papacy after Lando.

The aristocratic faction truly answered to the elder Theodora, Senator Theophylactus's wife. Liutprand of Cremona claims Theodora backed John's rise to hide an affair with him, a charge most writers rightly dismiss as slander. Liutprand, writing some fifty years on, slandered Romans he loathed without cease. At election time Theodora was old, and other writers praise her. John's kinship to Theodora's house explains her part in his election well enough.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-x:
Giovanni de' Medici ranked as Lorenzo the Magnificent's second son. He was marked for church life from boyhood. He became a cardinal at thirteen. He wore the rank's insignia only after three years. Leading humanists schooled him. He trained in theology and canon law at Pisa. In 1494 he fled Florence with his family. He then lived as a literary and artistic amateur.

He was elected pope in 1513. Leo poured money into art, letters, and St Peter's. Bramante led the rebuilding, and Raphael followed him. Sculpture languished under Leo. His mild temper failed to hold France and Venice in check. The long entry weighs his dazzling court against the storms gathering around it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-x:
Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto was born at Riese in 1835. His father was a postman who died in 1852. Giuseppe walked daily to the gymnasium at Castelfranco Veneto. He won a seminary scholarship at Padua and was ordained in 1858. For nine years he was chaplain at Tombolo, doing most of a parish priest's work for an aged pastor. As arch-priest of Salzano from 1867 he restored the church, funded the hospital, and served the poor through cholera.

As pope he struck at new theological methods rooted in agnosticism and immanentism, which he said stripped faith of objective, absolute truth. In 1907 his decree Lamentabili condemned sixty-five propositions, most on Scripture, Jesus, and the apostles. His encyclical Pascendi that September expounded and condemned Modernism across philosophy, history, liturgy, and discipline. It set rules for fighting doctrines he judged pernicious. The entry traces his campaign against Modernism through these documents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Frederick, later Stephen IX or X, was born early in the eleventh century and died at Florence on 29 March 1058. Gozelon, Duke of Lower Lorraine, and Junca, daughter of Berengarius II of Italy, were his parents. A canon of Liège, he became Leo IX's chancellor and librarian around 1051. He went with Leo on the 1054 embassy to Constantinople that ended in the East-West separation.

Robbed on his return by the Count of Teate, he dodged Henry III. Henry distrusted him as brother of the rebel Godfrey the Bearded. He became a monk at Monte Cassino in 1055 and its abbot in 1057. Victor II made him cardinal-priest of St Chrysogonus. On Victor's death he was chosen successor and consecrated the next day, 3 August 1057. As pope he carried on Leo IX's reform, making Peter Damian and Humbert cardinals at once and using Hildebrand, whom he sent to Milan.
doe-osti-17008692-optimization-analysis-: A research reactor collaboration got its game plan, and this optimization analysis plan covers the PRO-X and NCNR work on the NNS project. The text lays out the analytical approach. The reactor planners get their roadmap. The plan was written.
doe-osti-3007898-design-and-optimization: IMAGINE-X got designed, and this DOE text optimizes the NB1 diffractometer. The pages detail the findings. The neutron folks get their layout. The instrument was IMAGINE-X. The layout was neutron. The hall was NB1. The instrument was diffractometer.
doe-osti-3013903-surrogate-model-integra: MOOSE XFEM got surrogate-integrated, and this DOE text grows creep cracks by model. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their method. The growth was creep crack. The method was engineer. The code was MOOSE. The integration was surrogate.
the-duchess-of-berry-and-the-court-of-ch:
Imbert de Saint-Amand's The Duchess of Berry and the Court of Charles X maps the French court from 1824 on. Its contents run from the accession of Charles X, his entry into Paris, and the tombs of Saint-Denis to the coronation at Rheims, the jubilee of 1826, and the ministry of Polignac. Balls, reviews, and trips fill the middle.

At its heart stands Marie Caroline, the widowed Duchess of Berry, gay centre of court life. Saint-Amand writes with a royalist's warmth. The book shows a gay court dancing toward the fall of 1830.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-i-of: Here only the front pages and contents of volume one are shown, so the pieces themselves stay out of view. Marshall P. Wilder edited The Wit and Humor of America, a ten-volume set. Funk and Wagnalls published the Library Edition in New York and London. The contents list Oliver Wendell Holmes and The Deacon's Masterpiece. James Whitcomb Riley, Henry Ward Beecher, and Bayard Taylor also appear.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-ii-o: Volume two of The Wit and Humor of America survives here as front matter plus a contents list, with no pieces following. Marshall P. Wilder edited the ten-volume Library Edition for Funk and Wagnalls. A portrait of James Whitcomb Riley fronts the book. Harriet Beecher Stowe contributes Aunt Dinah's Kitchen. Other names include Robert J. Burdette, Henry P. Leland, and John B. Tabb.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-iii-: For volume three of The Wit and Humor of America, the pages present stop at the contents, leaving the selections unread here. Marshall P. Wilder edited the set, published by Funk and Wagnalls. A portrait of Samuel L. Clemens, Mark Twain, serves as frontispiece. Listed pieces include James Russell Lowell's The Courtin'. Charles Dudley Warner, Gelett Burgess, and Ellis Parker Butler also appear.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-iv-o: Nothing beyond the opening pages and contents of volume four appears in this record, so its humor pieces cannot be read here. Marshall P. Wilder edited The Wit and Humor of America for Funk and Wagnalls. Joel Chandler Harris is pictured at the front. The contents name Oliver Wendell Holmes and The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table. John G. Saxe, Sam Walter Foss, and Carolyn Wells are listed too.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-v-of: Volume five of The Wit and Humor of America is represented only by its opening matter and contents list in this record. Marshall P. Wilder edited the volume for Funk and Wagnalls. A note explains that this volume was not prepared from the Library Edition. Its page numbers therefore run differently from the other volumes. Thomas Bailey Aldrich is pictured, and James Whitcomb Riley appears in the contents.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-vi-o: In this record the sixth volume of The Wit and Humor of America shows its front matter and contents, but none of the pieces. Marshall P. Wilder edited the Library Edition for Funk and Wagnalls. Finley Peter Dunne, creator of Mr. Dooley, fronts the volume. The contents include Ernest Lawrence Thayer's Casey at the Bat. Eugene Field, John Hay, and F. Hopkinson Smith are also listed.
the-wit-and-humor-of-america-volume-vii-: The pages given for volume seven of The Wit and Humor of America end with the contents list, so the selections do not follow. Marshall P. Wilder edited the ten-volume set for Funk and Wagnalls. George Ade is the pictured author at the front. Charles Godfrey Leland's Breitmann pieces appear in the contents. Bill Nye, John Kendrick Bangs, and Ralph Waldo Emerson are listed as well.
tom-swift-and-the-visitor-from-planet-x:
Victor Appleton II's Tom Swift Jr. adventure is described on its dust jacket, printed here with cover and spine text. Tom and his associates at Swift Enterprises wait for the Planet X visitor, who comes as pure energy. The jacket calls it possibly the most important scientific event in history.

Tom has named the energy Exman, and hostile factions are determined to snatch it from his grasp. The book is number seventeen in the new Tom Swift Jr. adventures from Grosset and Dunlap. Readers get the publisher's own preview of a space-age invention story, presented as jacket copy rather than chapters.
